stem: About 48 hours after abruptly stopping heavy alcohol use, a client develops severe agitation, confusion, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, tremor, and tachycardia. Which complication should the nurse suspect most urgently?

options.A: Uncomplicated alcohol intoxication, because autonomic hyperactivity and tremor are expected after recent alcohol use rather than withdrawal.
options.B: Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder without delirium, because disorientation and marked autonomic hyperactivity exclude complicated withdrawal.
options.C: A mild uncomplicated alcohol-withdrawal syndrome that can be managed without close monitoring despite confusion and severe agitation.
options.D: Alcohol withdrawal delirium, requiring urgent evaluation, close monitoring, supportive care, and treatment for complicated withdrawal.

rationale: The current ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management guideline identifies autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, hallucinations, agitation, and seizures among alcohol-withdrawal features and describes alcohol withdrawal delirium as a complicated withdrawal state requiring close nursing observation and supportive care, frequent monitoring of vital signs, oximetry and cardiac status, and often intensive or critical care. Delirium commonly begins about 24 to 48 hours after cessation or reduction in alcohol use but may occur later. This client's severe agitation, confusion/disorientation, hallucinations, diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia, and 48-hour timing therefore make alcohol withdrawal delirium the most urgent complication to suspect. D is correct. The nurse must still evaluate for other causes of delirium rather than treating the vignette as a definitive diagnosis without assessment.
educational_objective: Recognize severe alcohol withdrawal with delirium, hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity as a medical emergency requiring urgent evaluation, close monitoring and treatment while excluding other causes of delirium.
source_document_title: The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management
source_version_date: Adopted January 23, 2020; remains the current ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management clinical guideline on the ASAM site in August 2026
source_locator: Alcohol withdrawal diagnostic criteria: autonomic hyperactivity, increased hand tremor, transient visual/tactile/auditory hallucinations, psychomotor agitation and seizures. Differential-diagnosis discussion: delirium requires medical/neurologic evaluation to rule out other causes; alcohol-withdrawal delirium typically occurs about 24-48 hours after cessation/reduction but can occur later. Recommendations VI.7-VI.13: close nursing observation/supportive care, continuous one-to-one observation for agitated/disoriented patients, frequent vital/oximetry/cardiac monitoring, IV access, and benzodiazepines as first-line treatment.
source_claim_supported: Severe agitation/confusion with hallucinations, tremor and autonomic hyperactivity about 48 hours after abrupt alcohol cessation is highly concerning for alcohol withdrawal delirium and requires urgent monitored management while alternative causes of delirium are evaluated.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: manage acute or life-threatening physical-health alterations, recognize complications of substance withdrawal, monitor unstable physiologic status and intervene for emergency changes in neurologic/cardiovascular function.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — complicated alcohol withdrawal and withdrawal delirium

source_original.stem: About 48 hours after abruptly stopping heavy alcohol use, a client develops severe agitation, confusion, visual hallucinations, diaphoresis, tremor, and tachycardia. Which complication should the nurse suspect most urgently?

options.A: Uncomplicated alcohol intoxication is most likely because autonomic hyperactivity and tremor are expected after recent drinking.
options.B: Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder without withdrawal is most likely because disorientation excludes complicated withdrawal.
options.C: The findings represent mild uncomplicated withdrawal that can be managed without close monitoring despite severe agitation and confusion.
options.D: Alcohol withdrawal delirium is strongly suggested and requires urgent monitored management of severe/complicated withdrawal.

source_original.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal delirium is a severe form of withdrawal characterized by delirium with autonomic hyperactivity and may include agitation and hallucinations. ASAM recommends close observation, frequent vital and cardiac monitoring, supportive care, and benzodiazepine-based treatment for alcohol withdrawal delirium.
source_original.source_detail: Alcohol withdrawal delirium: severe/complicated withdrawal with delirium, autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations/agitation; requires close monitoring and urgent treatment. Current ASAM guideline page and 2020 guideline remain active/current; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the complicated-alcohol-withdrawal construct and key D. Tightened D to emphasize urgent evaluation/monitoring rather than implying an unassessed definitive diagnosis, added the ASAM differential-diagnosis caveat, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a recognizable severe-withdrawal pattern plus emergency prioritization.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current ASAM Alcohol Withdrawal Management guideline; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: ASAM current clinical-guideline page live-rechecked 2026-08-16; 2020 alcohol-withdrawal guideline remains the active ASAM guideline
audit_findings.exact_locator: ASAM alcohol-withdrawal diagnostic criteria/differential discussion and Recommendations VI.7-VI.13 for alcohol withdrawal delirium
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item identifies the presentation as urgently concerning for alcohol withdrawal delirium without claiming the symptom cluster alone rules out other delirium etiologies; the timing and monitored-management claims are directly guideline-supported.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because the pattern follows cessation and includes classic withdrawal autonomic/neurologic features rather than uncomplicated intoxication.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because confusion/disorientation with autonomic hyperactivity supports complicated withdrawal; isolated alcohol-induced psychotic disorder is differentiated from delirium.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because severe confusion/agitation/hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity require close monitored management rather than classification as mild uncomplicated withdrawal.
distractor_audit.D: Correct and directly ASAM-supported as the most urgent complication to suspect/evaluate.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D integrates the withdrawal timing, delirium, hallucinations and marked autonomic activation while preserving the need to exclude other delirium causes.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives are alcohol-related interpretations of the same presentation, so the key is determined by severity, delirium and withdrawal physiology rather than an unrelated diagnosis.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — severe withdrawal, acute neurologic change and emergency monitoring.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the active ASAM guideline page, PDF diagnostic/differential text and rendered Recommendations VI.7-VI.13, all options, rationale, objective, timing, diagnostic caveat, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. D remained uniquely correct.
